children: By Ankur Banerjee

Asia's tech-heavy markets crumbled on Friday as fear of increased regulatory scrutiny and a slowdown in AI build-out unleashed the steepest decline in US stocks since the tariff-triggered "Liberation Day" rout in April 2025.
South Korea's KOSPI
fell more than 8% to trigger a circuit breaker and was last down 7% after trading resumed. Japan's Nikkei
slumped 6% while Taiwan
TWSE:TAIEX
was last down more than 8%.
Wall Street's volatility "fear gauge" soared
, the Nasdaq
sank 5.5% and $3 trillion was wiped off S&P 500 companies, with investors worried Democrats, who dominated the midterm elections this week, will apply the brakes to the AI boom.
The political jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky footing due to worries about the return on investment for the enormous sums of money being poured into the technology.
"There is also clearly an element of panic in the selling, and positioning is making the adjustment much more violent," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo.
"When investors begin unwinding these positions simultaneously, the selling can become self-reinforcing, particularly if leverage and forced liquidations are involved."
Market participants see Asia's chipmakers and data centre equipment suppliers in South Korea, Taiwan and Japan as especially vulnerable and they had already tumbled on Wednesday and Thursday.
AI chipmakers Samsung Electronics
fell nearly 10% while SK Hynix
slid 11.7%. Kioxia
plunged 14% while TSMC
was down 8.5%.
AI investor SoftBank Group
slid 11%, while the cost of insuring against a default for SoftBank jumped to its highest point in four years on Friday.
European stock futures
fell 1%, indicating that the selloff was likely to spread across to Europe.
REAL-TIME SENTIMENT SHIFT

Investor fear also centred on whether a stalling AI infrastructure expansion could hurt smaller firms whose capacity to raise funds has already been limited by higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions.
Neocloud company CoreWeave

, which has become a barometer of investor anxiety over heavy AI spending and borrowing, slumped 10%. Its 5-year credit default swap spreads (CRWV5YUSAX=MG), which measure market expectations of a potential default, widened to a record level.
"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift in sentiment," said Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo.

"Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that shows up in the market by huge swings in either direction," he said. "That's what we appear to have had  — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in."

The selling indicates investors are starting to factor in increased local opposition to building data centres, with analysts saying markets have yet to fully consider the cost such building has imposed on communities.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index
slumped 12.2% overnight and the Nasdaq, which reversed an initial swing higher after the midterms before dropping, has now shed 12% from its record high close a month ago.
Bonds were poised to gain in Asia, while the US dollar slipped against haven currencies such as the yen
and Swiss franc

"Treasuries can probably rally a lot further," said Nick Ferres, chief investment officer at Vantage Point Asset Management in Singapore. "And I suspect it will be an ugly day for semiconductor and memory (stocks)."
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note
was at 4.838%, hovering near the lowest level since September 9.
